## Today's Goals {.smaller}

Today we will

- More Modeling
  - Generating Predictions
  - Visually Evaluating Models
- Modeling in R
  - Implement a univariate linear model in R

We will use the CRU **and** FAO data

- `AGNR-AREC280_Fall2026/Data/CRU/parquet`
  - Filter to annual data
- `AGNR-AREC280_Fall2026/Data/FAO/parquet`
  - Filter to Avocado Yields
- Join on `Year` and `ISO3` into a single dataset




  
## Loading Datasets

First load the CRU and FAO data from Parquet Files

```{r load_fao}
#| echo: true
# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(arrow)
# Load the full fao dataset
read_parquet(
  file.path(data_path,"FAO","parquet","FAO_crop_livestock.parquet")
) |>
  filter(Item == "Avocados" & Element == "Yield") -> faostat_avocado

read_parquet(
  file.path(data_path,"CRU","parquet","tmp_w_ISO3.parquet")
) |>
  filter(Period == "ANN") -> cru_tmp_ann

faostat_avocado |>
  inner_join(cru_tmp_ann,join_by(ISO3,Year),suffix=c("_fao","_cru")) |>
  drop_na(ISO3) -> avocado_tmp
```

# Recap from last class 

## Modeling a single country

The country seems to matter a lot for yields

- We'll think about how to model country effects later
- Let's start off focusing on only Mexico
```{r filter-mexico}
#| echo: true
avocado_tmp |>
  filter(ISO3 == "MEX") -> avocado_tmp_mex
```



## Training an OLS Model

Train the following OLS model on the Mexico Avocado Yield data
$$Yield = b_0 + b_1 Temperature + \epsilon$$

```{r train-ols}
#| echo: true
lm(
  Value_fao ~ Value_cru,
  data=avocado_tmp_mex
) -> yield_model

print(yield_model)
```
```{r extract-params}
b0 = coefficients(yield_model)[["(Intercept)"]]
b1 = coefficients(yield_model)[["Value_cru"]]
pred_fn <- function(x) b0 + b1 * x
```



## Visualizing Our Model

```{r yield-plot-4}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
ggplot(data=avocado_tmp_mex,aes(x=Value_cru,y=Value_fao)) +
  geom_point(aes(color=Year),size=3) +
  geom_abline(
    intercept=coefficients(yield_model)[["(Intercept)"]],
    slope=coefficients(yield_model)[["Value_cru"]],
    color="red",linewidth=1.2
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x="Annual Average Temperature (C)",
    y="Yeild (mt/ha)",
    title="Avocado Yeilds in Mexico"
  ) +
  scale_color_viridis_c()
```

# Handling Model Output

## Using `moderndive`

The `moderndive` library adds a bunch of convienence functions for handling model output

- Wraps functions in the older `broom` library
- Designed to be consistent and easy-to-use
- You will need to install this package if you haven't already
```r
install.pacakges("moderndive")
```

# Formatting Output

## Model Output

- We trained a linear model
$$\hat y = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + \dots + b_n x_n$$
- Each feature $x_i$ has an associated parameter $b_i$
- Beyond the estimate of $b_i$ OLS determines other information
- Some is visible using `print()`, others require addional functions

## Formatting Model Output Using `moderndive`

Create a table of model parameters and other info using `get_regression_table(<model>)`

```{r show-reg-table}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
library(moderndive)
get_regression_table(yield_model)
```

## Understanding Model Output {.smaller}

```{r show-reg-table-2}
get_regression_table(yield_model)
```
What is this information?

- **term**: Name of the feature associated with this parameter ($x_i$)
- **estimate**: Model's estimated value of the parameter ($b_i$)
- **std_error**: A measure of the statistical uncertainty in the parameter estimate
- **statistic**: The [t-statistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-statistic) of a hypothesis test the true parameter is equal to zero
- **p_value**: The [p-value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-value) of this hypothesis test
- **lower_ci**: The lower bound of the 95% [Confidence Interval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confidence_interval) of the estimated parameter
- **upper_ci**: The upper bound of the 95% [Confidence Interval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confidence_interval) of the estimated parameter


## Interpreting Model Output - Warnings

Much of the information in this table relates to statistical properties of the estimated parameters

- This is not a course in econometrics or statistics
- We won't spend time formally defining these terms
- In particular, confidence intervals are a nuanced statistical concept
- In real-world data these values are likely "incorrect"
  - Need to be adjusted for peculiarities of your data
  - Used as-is would lead to incorrect conclusions

## Interpreting Model Output - Standard Error

For the purposes of this class

- **std_error** is the [Standard Error](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_error) of the parameter estimate
- Measure of the precision of the estimated parameter
- Small values indicate high precision
- Adding more data or running the analysis on new data unlikely to 
substantially alter the estimate of the parameter
- Small standard errors increase your confidence you have a reliable estimate

## Interpreting Model Output - Confidence Intervals

For the purposes of this class

- **lower_ci** and **upper_ci** are bounds on the 95% confidence interval of the estimated parameter
- A measure of the range of parameter values you might have seen
- The model's best guess of
  - If you collected new data and repeated this process many times
  - 95% of the parameter estimates would fall in this range
- Narrow confidence intervals increase your confidence you have a reliable estimate
- Suggest estimates outside that range are unlikely



## Formatting table output

You can request [Markdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markdown) formatted output
by setting `print=TRUE`

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
get_regression_table(yield_model,print=TRUE)
```

Gives output
```{r show-reg-table-kable-2}
#| echo: false
get_regression_table(yield_model,print=TRUE) |> writeLines()
```

## Formatting table output - Markdown {.smaller}

The provided markdown renders to something like this
```{r show-reg-table-kable}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
get_regression_table(yield_model,print=TRUE)
```
Create a table in 

- [Google Docs](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/12014036?hl=en) with "Paste as Markdown"
- MS Word requires third-party plugins


# Generating Model Predictions

## Model Predictions

- We have a trained OLS model
$$Yield = `r format(b0,scientific = FALSE,digits=5)` + `r format(b1,scientific = FALSE,digits=5)` \cdot Temperature + \epsilon$$
- Implies a **prediction** for each observation
- Our best guess of the label given the features and this model
- We can construct predictions by hand using this formula
- Or use `get_regression_points()`

## Using `moderndive` {.smaller}

```{r get-predictions}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
get_regression_points(yield_model) -> yield_model_points
print(yield_model_points)
```


## Evaluating Model Predictions

```{r eval-predictions-viz}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
ggplot(yield_model_points) +
  geom_point(aes(x=Value_fao,y=Value_fao_hat),color="black",size=1.5) +
  geom_abline(slope=1,intercept=0,color="red",linewidth=1) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title="Modeled Yields for Mexico",
    x="Actual Yield",
    y="Predicted Yield"
  )
```

## Applying the Model

```{r subset-columbia}
#| echo: true
avocado_tmp |>
  filter(ISO3 == "COL") -> avocado_tmp_col
```

## Use model to predict

```{r predict-col}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
get_regression_points(yield_model,newdata=avocado_tmp_col) -> forecast_col
print(forecast_col)
```

## Visualize Predictions
```{r eval-predictions-viz-col}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
ggplot(forecast_col) +
  geom_point(aes(x=Value_fao,y=Value_fao_hat),color="black",size=1.5) +
  geom_abline(slope=1,intercept=0,color="red",linewidth=1) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title="Modeled Yields for Columbia",
    x="Actual Yield",
    y="Predicted Yield"
  )
```
